title: UAE Travel Alert: US, UK, Canada and Australia Renew Middle East Warnings as Airlines Adjust Routes
excerpt: Multiple Western governments have updated travel advisories for the Gulf region as the Iran conflict disrupts aviation corridors and maritime shipping routes.
body:
• The US, UK, Canada, and Australia have renewed or upgraded travel warnings for the UAE and wider Gulf region as the Iran conflict enters its third week.
  • Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Emirates have adjusted flight routes to avoid conflict zones, with some services experiencing delays and cancellations.
  • Brent crude has surged past $100 per barrel after Houthi strikes on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, extending the conflict to a second major shipping chokepoint.
  • Dubai has responded by offering $800 in travel perks to visitors as tourism numbers decline sharply.

Multiple Western governments have updated their travel advisories for the United Arab Emirates and the broader Middle East as the US-Iran conflict and associated Houthi attacks on shipping routes continue to escalate, creating complications for millions of travelers who transit through the Gulf's major aviation hubs.

What the Advisories Say

The United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia have all renewed warnings urging citizens to exercise heightened caution when traveling to the UAE and surrounding countries. While the UAE itself has not been directly targeted in the conflict, its proximity to Iran — just 150 kilometers across the Strait of Hormuz — and its role as a critical global aviation hub have prompted governments to flag elevated risks.

The advisories warn of potential disruptions to air travel, the risk of missile or drone strikes affecting nearby airspace, and the possibility of rapid security deterioration that could strand travelers.

Airlines Adjust Routes

Major Gulf carriers Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Emirates have adjusted flight paths to avoid conflict zones, routing some flights around Iranian airspace. The changes have added flight time to certain routes and led to scattered delays and cancellations, particularly on routes between Asia and Europe that typically overfly the region.

Emirates, the UAE's flagship carrier, recently debuted its new U-Dream headrest for economy class passengers — a move analysts note coincides with efforts to maintain traveler confidence amid the security challenges.

Dubai's tourism authorities have responded to declining visitor numbers by offering $800 in travel perks to visitors, including hotel credits, attraction passes, and dining vouchers — a sign of how directly the regional instability is hitting the emirate's tourism-dependent economy.

Oil Prices and Economic Fallout

The conflict's economic impact widened sharply this week after Houthi fighters struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, extending the war to a second major shipping chokepoint. President Trump responded by promising "major military punishment" for Iran and its Houthi allies.

Brent crude surged past $100 per barrel for the first time since the conflict began, with immediate consequences for India — the world's third-largest crude importer. Indian markets fell for a fifth straight session on Friday, with the Sensex shedding over 330 points as oil prices stoked inflation fears.

What NRI Travelers Should Know

The UAE remains a critical transit point for Indians traveling between the US, Europe, and India. Emirates, Etihad, and Air India all operate major connecting services through Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Travelers with upcoming bookings should:

  • Monitor airline communications for route changes and potential delays
  • Check government travel advisories before departure and register with embassy notification systems
  • Consider travel insurance that covers conflict-related disruptions
  • Allow extra time for connections, particularly on eastbound routes through the Gulf

The situation remains fluid, with the US, Iran, and regional actors engaged in both military operations and intermittent diplomatic contacts. Travelers should be prepared for advisories to change on short notice.
